title: The six verb types
goal: Complete the whole present-tense verb system of Finnish — six types, six ways to build the stem, and after this unit there's no verb you can't conjugate yourself.
bekal: recognize a verb's type from its dictionary form alone
build the stem for all six types and add the personal endings
talk about free-time activities and hobbies

dialogs.title: Dialog — Mitä sinä harrastat?
dialogs.intro: The weekend is coming. Marek, Aino and Budi talk about what they do in their free time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pelaan jalkapalloa ja soitan kitaraa. Entä sinä?
lines.id: I play football and play the guitar. And you?
lines.literal: play-I football-part and play-I guitar-part. and you?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Minä juoksen. Ja talvella hiihdän — yritän ainakin.
lines.id: I run. And in winter I ski — or at least I try.
lines.literal: I run. and in-winter ski-I — try-I at-least.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Minä valitsen aina helpomman: käyn kahvilassa ja luen.
lines.id: I always choose the easier option: I go to a café and read.
lines.literal: I choose always easier-one: go-I in-café and read-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sekin on harrastus! Tarvitsetko sinä kirjastokorttia?
lines.id: That's a hobby too! Do you need a library card?
lines.literal: that-too is hobby! need-? you library-card-part?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Minulla on jo. Se on ilmainen — Suomessa kirjastot ovat pyhiä.
lines.id: I already have one. It's free — in Finland libraries are sacred.
lines.literal: at-me is already. it is free — in-Finland libraries are sacred-part.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Totta. Tapaan usein ystäviä kirjastossa, emmekä edes lue.
lines.id: True. I often meet friends at the library, and we don't even read.
lines.literal: true. meet-I often friends-part in-library, and-not-we even read.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you want to come and play on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Minä tulen katsomaan. En osaa pelata ollenkaan.
lines.id: I'll come and watch. I can't play at all.
lines.literal: I come to-watch. not-I can play at-all.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Minä tulen. Mutta minä vanhenen — juoksen hitaasti nykyään.
lines.id: I'll come. But I'm getting old — I run slowly these days.
lines.literal: I come. but I grow-old — run-I slowly nowadays.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Me kaikki vanhenemme. Se ei ole tekosyy!
lines.id: We're all getting older. That's no excuse!
lines.literal: we all grow-old-we. it not is excuse!

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.id: Well said. See you Saturday on the field!

notes: **Tapaan, not tavaan.** Type 4 verbs gradate **in reverse**: the dictionary form is weak (*tavata*), the personal forms are strong (*tapaan*). It's the opposite of the type 1 you learned in unit 8, and the only part of the verb system that can really trip you up.

**Tarvitsen from tarvita.** Type 5 inserts *-tse-*, which is completely invisible in the dictionary form. Luckily the group is small; the only really common ones are *tarvita* (need), *valita* (choose) and *häiritä* (disturb).

**Vanhenen from vanheta.** Type 6 inserts *-ne-* and nearly all its verbs mean "to become more…": *vanheta* (grow old), *kylmetä* (get colder), *pimetä* (get darker). The smallest type — you could live for years without it.

**Pelaamaan, katsomaan** — the "in order to do" form. After verbs of motion (*tulla*, *mennä*, *lähteä*), the next verb takes *-maan/-mään*: *tulen katso**maan*** (I'm coming to watch). Compare *haluan katso**a***, which uses the dictionary form. The choice depends on the first verb, and it's one of the things that takes longest to get used to.
**Emmekä edes lue** — *ja* becomes *-kä* in negative sentences, as you learned in unit 7. Note *lue* too, the bare form of *lukea*.

**Soitan kitaraa** literally means "I sound the guitar". *Soittaa* is used for playing instruments **and** for phoning: *soitan sinulle* (I'll call you). Playing games uses *pelata*: *pelaan jalkapalloa*. English uses "play" for both, so this is a distinction to keep in mind.

grammars.title: The six verb types
body: Every Finnish verb belongs to one of these six types, and you can tell which one straight from **the last two letters of the dictionary form**. Once the stem is built, the personal endings are the same for every type.
after: **Types 1 and 3 cover most of everyday conversation.** Type 2 is small but very frequent (*juoda*, *syödä*, *saada*, *tuoda*, *viedä*, *käydä*). Types 5 and 6 can wait; both are rare.
⚠️ Type 3 always has a stem ending in **-e-**, so its *hän* form lengthens the *e*: *tulee*, *menee*, *nousee*, *opiskelee*. This is the form beginners mispronounce most often — two *e*'s, not one.
Type 2 doesn't lengthen anything in the *hän* form, because the stem already ends in a long vowel or a diphthong: *hän juo*, *hän syö*, *hän saa*.

grammars.title: Reverse gradation in type 4
body: Type 4 is the only one that goes against the instinct you built in unit 8. Here the dictionary form is **weak** and the personal forms are **strong**.
after: Look at *tavata → tapaan*: *v* becomes *p*, gradating the other way round. Likewise *herätä → herään* (the *t* disappears) and *hypätä → hyppään* (*p* becomes *pp*).
You've been using four verbs of this type since the early units without knowing their type: *haluta*, *osata*, *tavata*, *herätä*. Now you know why their forms seem to jump.
⚠️ The *hän* form adds no extra vowel because the stem already ends in a double vowel: *hän tapaa*, not *tapaaa*.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Olla* belongs to type 3, but it's still irregular: its *hän* form is *on*, not *olee*. It's the only truly rebellious verb in Finnish, and you've known it by heart since unit 1.
⚠️ What you play is always partial: *pelaan jalkapallo**a***, *soitan kitara**a***. Same reason as reading a book — playing is an ongoing activity, never "fully finished".

blocks.title: Asking about hobbies
items: *Mitä sinä harrastat?* — What are your hobbies?
*Mitä sinä teet vapaa-ajalla?* — What do you do in your free time?
*Käytkö sinä usein…?* — Do you often go to…?

*Marjastaminen* and *sienestäminen* (berry and mushroom picking) are serious national hobbies. The law of *jokamiehenoikeus* (everyman's right) lets anyone pick in any forest, even on private land — as long as they don't come close to the owner's house.
See you Saturday on the field.
